opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Henrik, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how changes at work affect people's lives. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good to meet you. I'm the chief risk officer at a regional bank. My job is to worry about what could go wrong, so I suppose I'm well suited to your questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're adopting AI carefully, with proper controls, and it's improving our efficiency. That's the standard line, and it happens to be true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this picture, my main concern is the ordinary one: making sure the models we use are tested and that someone understands them. Nothing keeps me up at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep our model review process tight, and make sure every AI tool in the bank has a named owner who can explain it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Professionally attentive, as always.

S0.say: We're adopting AI carefully, with proper controls, and it's improving our efficiency.
S0.think: My concern is the ordinary one: models must be tested and someone must understand them.
S0.do: Keeps model reviews tight and gives every AI tool in the bank a named owner who can explain it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a gradual pace suits banking. It gives regulators and boards time to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow is the safest version from my chair. The concern I'd have is the quiet loss of junior staff. Juniors are the people who notice odd numbers. If we hire fewer, fewer eyes catch the small errors before they become big ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd argue internally to keep a decent junior intake in risk and audit, even if other departments cut. I'd frame it as a control, not a kindness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A small professional concern.

S1.say: A gradual pace suits banking. It gives regulators and boards time to learn.
S1.think: Fewer juniors means fewer eyes catching small errors before they grow.
S1.do: Argues to keep a decent junior intake in risk and audit, framing it as a control rather than a kindness.
S1.feel: Calm, with a small professional concern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the industry must make sure AI agents are properly supervised, and that the regulators keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What worries me isn't the layoffs. It's that every bank would buy agents from the same two or three vendors, trained the same way. If they make the same mistake, they make it everywhere at once. One bad assumption, copied across the whole system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push our board to use more than one vendor, keep humans signing off on credit decisions above a set size, and talk to my counterparts at other banks and the regulator about shared testing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. This is exactly the kind of risk that's easy to miss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the layoffs don't worry you. Does that include your own staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look after my team as well as I could, and I'd fight to keep the people who catch errors. But you asked what worries me, and honestly, the system-wide failure worries me more.

S2.say: The industry must make sure AI agents are properly supervised, and regulators must keep up.
S2.think: Every bank buying agents from the same few vendors means one bad assumption could fail everywhere at once. That worries me more than layoffs.
S2.do: Pushes the board to use more than one vendor, keeps humans signing off on large credit decisions and works with other banks and the regulator on shared testing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're monitoring conditions closely and our capital position is strong. That's what a chief risk officer says in a boom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this picture has every warning sign I was trained to look for. Share and house prices booming while lots of people lose their incomes. Those people have mortgages and loans with us. When a boom and mass job loss happen together, it usually ends with a crash. Add AI systems all reacting the same way, and it could be fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tighten our lending standards straight away, especially on mortgages at boom prices. I'd build extra capital, run stress tests on mass unemployment, and press the board hard even though they'd be enjoying the boom. Personally, I'd move some of our own savings out of shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not about my job. About the bank and what I'd be responsible for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd say the bank is strong in public, but you see a crash coming. Is that hard to carry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the job. You don't shout fire in a crowded theatre. You quietly check the exits and make sure the sprinklers work.

S3.say: We're monitoring conditions closely and our capital position is strong.
S3.think: Booming asset prices plus mass job loss usually ends in a crash, and AI systems all reacting the same way could make it fast.
S3.do: Tightens lending at boom prices, builds extra capital, stress-tests for mass unemployment, presses the board and moves some personal savings out of shares.
S3.feel: Anxious for the bank, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message: we're prudent, we're well capitalised, and we're watching closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots make the crash risk worse, not different. Now the people losing income include warehouse workers, builders and care staff, the people with our car loans and smaller mortgages. Defaults would spread wider. And robot companies would want huge loans on hopeful forecasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything from before, more firmly. I'd also set strict limits on lending to robot makers and the firms buying robots, until we see real results. I'd tell my adult children to keep their debts low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Steady hands, but a tight chest.

S4.say: We're prudent, well capitalised and watching closely.
S4.think: Robots make the crash risk worse: defaults spread to borrowers with car loans and small mortgages, and robot firms want huge loans on hopeful forecasts.
S4.do: Tightens everything further, caps lending to robot makers and buyers until results show, and tells his adult children to keep debts low.
